en: Now, *Abhijñānaśākuntalam*. Act One:
She who is the primordial creation of the Creator, she who carries the oblation offered according to the ritual rules, and she who is the priestess of the sacrifice—

May the Lord protect you with those eight perceptible forms by which he ordains the two times, which possesses qualities that pervade the universe as the object of the Vedas, which they call the primordial nature (*prakṛti*) containing all seeds, and by which living beings possess life. 1.1. p.2.
Director: Noble sir, this assembly is composed mostly of discerning people.
Today, we must present a new drama called *Abhijñānaśākuntala*, with its plot woven by Kālidāsa.
Therefore, let care be taken for each individual role.
Actress: By virtue of the noble one’s well-rehearsed performance, nothing at all shall be left to laughter.
Director: [Continues]
Noble lady, I shall tell you the truth of the matter:
I do not consider a mastery of performance to be truly successful until it satisfies the learned;
for even among those who are highly trained, the mind remains distrustful of itself.
Nati: Noble sir, it is even so.
May the noble sir command what must be done next.
Sūtradhāra: What else [could there be] than pleasing the ears of this assembly?
Therefore, let this very summer season— which has recently begun and is fit for enjoyment— be celebrated in song.
For now,
the waters are delightful to plunge into, and the forest breezes are fragrant from contact with the *pāṭala* flowers.
The days are pleasant at their close, when sleep is easily found in the deep shade.
Nati: So be it. (She sings:
"Adorning themselves with care, young women wear the *śirīṣa* flowers, whose delicate filaments have been only slightly kissed by bees."
Sūtradhāra: Noble sir, well sung! Oh, the entire audience has its heart and mind so bound by passion that it is as if painted there. Therefore, upon what play shall we now rely to please them?
Nati: But surely the noble gentlemen were already commanded that the unprecedented play named *Abhijñānaśākuntalam* should be undertaken for performance?
Sūtradhāra: Noble lady, I have been rightly reminded;
at this moment, indeed, I had forgotten it. Why is that?
"I have been forcibly carried away by the captivating melody of your song,
just as King Duṣyanta was by the deer with its excessive speed."
(Thus they both exit. (End of the Prologue. (Then enters the King, pursuing a deer with bow and arrow in hand, together with his charioteer in a chariot.)
Charioteer: (Looking at the King and the deer) Long-lived one!
With your eye fixed upon the black antelope and your bow strung, I seem to behold the wielder of the Pināka bow himself in person as he pursues the deer.
The King: Charioteer, we have been drawn far away by this deer;
yet even now, he repeatedly casts his gaze back at the chariot, making it beautiful with the way he turns his neck.
Having entered with his hindquarters mostly drawn forward for fear of the falling arrows,
his path strewn with half-chewed *darbha* grass dropping from his mouth which is agape from exhaustion—
behold, because of his high leaping, he travels much further in the air and but little upon the earth. (Śākuntala 1.7)
(With astonishment) How is it that he has become difficult for me to behold, even as I am pursuing him?
Charioteer: My lord, because the ground was uneven, I slackened the speed of the chariot by pulling in the reins.
Therefore, this deer has become far removed;
now that you are on level ground, he will not be difficult to reach.
King: In that case, let the reins be loosened.
Charioteer: As Your Majesty commands.
(Observing the speed of the chariot) Your Majesty, look, look!
When the reins were loosened, with their forebodies stretched forward,
their chowrie-tips motionless and their ears pricked up and still,
they could not be overtaken even by the dust raised by themselves.
"These horses are galloping as if on a chariot-track made of the very speed of deer.
King: Truly so!
The steeds have surpassed both the directions and the sun's horses. For thus it is:
That which is subtle in the light suddenly attains expansion;
that which is severed in the middle appears as if joined together;
and that which is naturally curved in the eyes is also perfectly straight in its lines.
Nothing is far from me, nor even for a moment, due to the speed of the chariot.

The word of the Brahmin has been accepted. Vaikhānasa: O King, we have set out to gather sacrificial fuel. Indeed, here is the hermitage of Kaṇva, the head of the clan, visible along the bank of the Mālinī river.
If there is no pressing engagement with other duties, please enter and accept this hospitality due to a guest. Moreover,
having observed the delightful rites of those whose wealth is asceticism, which have been rendered free from obstacles,
you shall know how far my arm— marked by the scars of the bowstring— protects them.
King: Is the head of the community present here?
Vaikhānasa: He has just now departed for Somatīrtha to appease adverse fate, having appointed his daughter Śakuntalā to attend to the hospitality of guests.
King: Very well.
I see her indeed;
she will surely make my devotion known to the Great Seer.
Vaikhānasa: We shall depart for now. (Thus he exits with his disciples.)
King: Charioteer, urge on the horses; let us purify ourselves by beholding this holy hermitage. Charioteer: As the long-lived one commands. (He drives the chariot accordingly once more.)
King—(Looking all around):
Charioteer, even though it has not been told to me, it is evident that this expanse belongs to a penance grove.
Charioteer: How so?

King: Do you not see? For here, indeed—beneath the trees, there are grains of wild rice fallen from the openings of hollows containing parrots; in some places, smooth stones are visible, having split the shells of *iṅgudī* fruits.
The deer, having gained confidence, move without fear and endure the sound [of our approach];
and the paths along the water-holding channels are marked by lines of dripping resin from the bark garments.
The roots of the trees have been washed by the waters of the rivulets, trembling in the wind; the redness of the young shoots has been altered by the rising smoke of the clarified butter;
and here, in the nearby garden grounds, the sprouts of darbha grass have been cut down.
The fawns, having lost their way, wander very slowly. Charioteer: Everything is consistent with this. King: (Having gone a short distance)
"Let there be no disturbance to those dwelling in the penance grove.
Halt the chariot at this very spot while I descend.
Charioteer: The reins are held.
"May the venerable one descend. The King—(descending):
Charioteer, one must enter the so-called penance groves in humble attire.
"Let this much be accepted for now.
(Having brought forth the charioteer's ornaments and his bow, he hands them over.
"Charioteer, let the horses have their backs rubbed until they are moist while I return after inspecting those dwelling in the hermitage."
Sūta: So be it. (He exits.
King: (Walking about and looking around) Here is the entrance to the hermitage.
Just as I am entering— (having entered,
indicating an omen)—
this hermitage is tranquil, yet my arm throbs; from where can there be fruit for this?
Or rather, doors of destiny are everywhere.

"Whoever desires to make this naturally charming body capable of enduring ascetic toil surely intends, as a sage, to cut down a śamī creeper with the edge of a blue lotus petal. Very well; let me watch her from behind this tree for now.

In this matter, reproach your own youth for causing the expansion of your breasts;
why do you reproach me? King: Granted, the bark garment is ill-suited to this form, yet it does not fail to foster the beauty of its ornamentation. Why so?
A lotus is beautiful even when entwined with moss;
the spot on the moon, though dark, spreads its splendor. This slender woman is even more enchanting, though clad in bark.
For what indeed is not an ornament for those whose forms are sweet?

That is why you are truly Priyaṃvadā. King: Priyaṃvadā speaks words that are both pleasant and true to Śakuntalā.
Indeed,
her lower lip has the hue of a young sprout, her arms resemble tender branches,
and youth, as alluring as a flower, has taken its place upon her limbs. (KSak_1.19)
